segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Gita's first chapter: drishtva, having seen. Duryodhana looked first, and the verb waited at the end. Now he opens his mouth.

A message lands in the family group chat: great planning by our star student. Is it praise? Is it a jab? Everyone reads it twice, and nobody types back for a while. Now the scene. Duryodhana stands in front of his teacher, Drona, and points across the field at the army drawn up against him. His first word is an order: pashya. Look. A prince is telling his own teacher where to look. And the sting hasn't even arrived yet. It's waiting at the end of the line, where Sanskrit likes to keep its surprises.
screen: `PRAISE, OR A JAB?` → `A PRINCE AND HIS TEACHER.` → `PASHYA: LOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: pashyaitam panduputranam acharya mahatim chamum. Pashyaitam is two words run together: pashya, look, and etam, this. Sanskrit lets sounds melt at the seam, and part of reading is pulling them apart again. Then acharya. Yesterday it was acharyam, the teacher as the one Duryodhana went up to. Today the ending is gone, and acharya means O teacher. That bare form is how Sanskrit calls out to someone. English does it with an O, or a name and a comma; Sanskrit does it by changing the word itself. So: look, O teacher, at this great army of Pandu's sons. Now the second half: vyudham drupadaputrena tava shishyena dhimata. Drawn up by Drupada's son, your student, the wise one. The ending -ena means by. And there's the barb. The army facing Drona was arranged by a man Drona taught. Tava, your. Shishyena, by the student. Dhimata, by the wise one. Duryodhana could have said the enemy commander. He says your clever pupil. Some readers hear worry in it, a prince afraid his teacher's heart is divided. Some hear a prince needling the man who trained his enemy. The words don't settle it. But the Sanskrit lets him save the blow for last, right where a listener's ear is waiting.
screen: `PASHYA + ETAM: LOOK AT THIS.` · `ACHARYA: O TEACHER.` · `-ENA: BY.` · `YOUR STUDENT, THE WISE ONE.` · then, large: `THE BARB COMES LAST.`

segments.voice: Say the first half of the line once, out loud or under your breath: pashyaitam panduputranam acharya mahatim chamum. Then rest on the word acharya, and let a teacher from your own life come to mind, just the face, with no story attached, for the rest of the sit. If no face comes, let the word itself be enough.
Reading the Gita's first chapter: today, pashya, look, and acharya, O teacher, the bare form Sanskrit uses to call someone. One verse, a look and a jab.

howItsDone: Some Hindus study the Gita verse by verse with a teacher, saying each line aloud before working through its words; in Hindu tradition the acharya, the teacher, is honored.

fork.setup: at a tournament, your coach points out the rival captain: 'your old teammate, the clever one, set up their defense.' read like Gita 1.3, what is the line doing?
options: naming the captain plainly, nothing more.
saving a pointed detail for last, where it stings.
praising you for training the captain.
fork.reveal: Duryodhana names the enemy's arranger as tava shishyena dhimata, your student, the wise one: the pointed detail, set last.

original.note: Sanskrit: acharya, teacher; in this verse, the calling form, O teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: acharya is just a polite title, like professor.
what it means: teacher; here it's the calling form, O teacher, said to Drona.
what a scholar hears: a vocative with no ending, beside -ena instrumentals that put the barb, your student, last.

chat.says: Uncle Vikram replied to dad's party plan: 'great planning by nani's favorite.' compliment or not??
options: could be either, like 'your student' in Gita 1.3: the barb sits last. ask, don't assume.
a compliment, clearly; 'favorite' is a warm word, so there's no barb in it at all.
an attack, clearly; when a sting comes at the end, nothing before it counts.
chat.meaning: In Gita 1.3 Duryodhana calls the enemy's arranger tava shishya, your student: readers hear worry or needling. The words don't settle it, so asking beats assuming.
